brief_summary: Diagram of a single 60% PCB's bottom-left corner showing the ANSI and ISO switch-position footprints side by side within one shared dashed bounding box. ANSI shows a wide 2.25u left-shift position; ISO shows a narrower 1.25u shift plus one additional switch position, with the position that doesn't apply to a given build shown as a dashed, unpopulated outline. Illustrates the article's claim that one PCB tooling run covered both bottom-row conventions.
data_sources: 60-percent-layout-history.mdx § 'Why 60% specifically won' — 'GH60 supported both ANSI and ISO layouts from the same board by including switch-position footprints for both bottom-row conventions and leaving whichever set didn't apply unpopulated... a single PCB tooled to cover both markets meant a vendor didn't have to run two separate manufacturing lines to sell into North America and Europe.'

GeekHack wiki GH60 page (cited in article via <Source>) — documents ANSI and ISO layout variants including 1.50x and 1.25x bottom-row widths, describing GH60 as 'the first ISO 60% mechanical keyboard.'
